implementation_notes: Scala 2.13's collections added an explicit in-place family for mutable buffers: filterInPlace(p) replaces the buffer's contents with the filtered result and returns this, so it chains with the other *InPlace operations. The 2.13 Buffer source implements it as the pattern's own compaction loop - a read index and a write index copying survivors down, then takeInPlace(j) to truncate once - which is the same shape C++ reaches with remove_if plus erase, delivered by the container itself. ArrayBuffer is the usual concrete choice; dropInPlace, takeInPlace and sliceInPlace handle prefix, suffix and range removals, and subtractOne or -= remove single values. Prefer filterInPlace when the buffer is a private mutable accumulator whose identity matters (a scheduler queue, a tick buffer, a builder reused across frames); it is one pass with no allocation, unlike calling remove in a loop.
code_sketch:
import scala.collection.mutable
val buf = mutable.ArrayBuffer(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
buf.filterInPlace(_ % 2 == 1)   // ArrayBuffer(1, 3, 5), in place, O(n)
buf.dropInPlace(1)              // ArrayBuffer(3, 5)
pitfalls: filterInPlace keeps where the predicate is true - the same direction as Rust's retain and the opposite of a remove_if-style API - so mixing it with copied predicates is a classic polarity bug.

The *InPlace family is defined on mutable.Buffer/IndexedBuffer (ArrayBuffer, ListBuffer, ArrayDeque); immutable List/Vector/Seq only offer filter/filterNot, which build a new collection, and the two return different things (this versus a new value).
In-place mutation is visible to every alias of the buffer, so a shared ArrayBuffer cannot be compacted without synchronisation - the standard aliasing hazard that the immutable form does not have.

variants.name: immutable filterNot / filter (persistent rebuild)
variants.implementation_notes: Idiomatic Scala usually does not mutate at all: the erase-remove outcome is expressed as filterNot(pred), or filter with the complementary predicate, on an immutable List/Vector/Set, which builds the new value in one pass with structural sharing and leaves the original untouched - the same result at the cost of one new root object, no aliasing, and no observability question. It is the right default whenever the sequence is a value (a function argument, a case-class field, anything crossing a boundary), and it composes directly with map/flatMap/collect chains. Reach for the mutable *InPlace family only when profiling shows the rebuild dominates and the collection is a private accumulator.
variants.code_sketch:
val xs = List(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
val kept = xs.filterNot(_ % 2 == 0)   // List(1, 3, 5); xs unchanged
val also = xs.filter(_ % 2 == 1)      // same set, predicate inverted
pitfalls: filterNot(p) and filter(p) are complements: swapping them without negating the predicate silently keeps the elements that were meant to go.

The immutable form allocates a new top-level structure per rebuild (structural sharing bounds the cost but not the new root), so inside a hot loop over a mutable accumulator it is exactly the allocation filterInPlace avoids.
